 Open Navigation Menu Menu The Lede Anthropic and the Monetization of Paradise
 What does it mean to sell shares in the idea of a better world? Ahead of its I.P.O., the company is making the pitch. By Jill Lepore November 18, 2026 Illustration by Dan Zhou Save this story Save this story Save this story Save this story The Earth is still twirling on its axis as it glides across the heavens in its elegant orbit of the sun, but Anthropic’s stock goes up for sale this week, so brace yourself for a certain planetary chaos: money falling from the skies, the sense of time stopped—at least, if the grandiose promises in the company’s S-1 filing are to be believed. Beginning on Thursday morning, when the opening bell rings on Wall Street, you will be able to invest in “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” O brave new world, that has such publicly traded stock in it.
 The Lede 
 Reporting and commentary on what you need to know today. 
 “We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning,” the company states in the filing. Anthropic is a public-benefit corporation, and its S-1 must abide by rules set by the S.E.C.; it is required to disclose risks and to explain how its goals for benefitting the public—humanity!—may affect shareholder profits. Compared with the Silicon Valley venture-capital hype of the Andreessen Horowitz variety, then, the rhetoric of Anthropic’s three-hundred-plus-page stock prospectus is restrained, and even cautious. The company, for instance, acknowledges that its technology “may pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” and that, even if Claude doesn’t kill everyone, public concern that it might “could adversely affect our reputation and brand.” Caveat emptor.
 Of course, most of the filing concerns the prospects for profit, on the back of the promise that, “if managed well,” A.I. “could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort.” Is Anthropic attempting to monetize the idea of paradise?
 The company’s I.P.O. puts me in mind of a call for investment issued nearly two centuries ago, offering “small shares of twenty dollars” to anyone willing to join an “association for the improvement of the human condition.” This prospectus came in the form of a treatise published in Pittsburgh, in 1833, titled “ The Paradise Within the Reach of All Men, Without Labour, by Powers of Nature and Machinery: An Address to All Intelligent Men .” Its author, a German engineer and inventor named John Adolphus Etzler who had immigrated to the U.S., claimed that solar, wind, and sea power could make the struggle for human existence obsolete. “FELLOW-MEN!” he began, “I promise to show the means for creating a paradise within ten years, where every thing desirable for human life may be had for every man in superabundance, without labour, without pay; where the whole face of nature is changed into the most beautiful form of which it be capable,” a world where a man “may provide himself with means unheard of yet, for increasing his knowledge of the world, and so his intelligence; he may lead a life of continual happiness, of enjoyments unknown yet; he may free himself from almost all the evils that afflict mankind, except death, and even put death far beyond the common period of human life, and, finally, render it less afflicting.”
 Anthropic’s bid for shareholders rests, by decided contrast, on real, working machinery, the ingenious, unsettling advances that fall under the heading of artificial intelligence: “For the first time in history, intelligence is something humans can build.” Yet the premise of the Anthropic offering—invest in the possibility of paradise—is strikingly similar to Etzler’s technological utopianism. Anthropic proposes to “significantly accelerate global growth and dramatically improve quality of life for people around the world.” So did Etzler.
 In the prospectus, Anthropic—presumably keen to avoid the vague and controversial language of “artificial general intelligence” and “superintelligence”—refers, instead, to “Powerful AI.” By this, it means to describe artificial intelligence with “cognitive capabilities matching or exceeding those of top human experts across most professional and scientific disciplines” and possessing “the ability to interface with the physical world,” by way of robots and other devices. Achieving Powerful A.I. is Anthropic’s goal, one that it envisions accomplishing, chiefly, by way of Claude, which is fast improving itself. (“Each new version of a Claude model directly accelerates development of the next.”) The enormous investment that will almost certainly result from the I.P.O. will also allow Anthropic to “expand our own data center footprint,” necessary for the scale of compute required for the company’s growth, in both existing markets and new ones: “reaching domains from healthcare and life sciences to robotics and the physical world.” (To picture how all this will work, it’s important to set aside the idea that Claude is a chatbot on your laptop. For instance, Claude will revolutionize medical research because Claude and its minions may soon be able to run an entire lab: “our Model Hardware Standard enables AI agents to operate lab and manufacturing equipment such as microscopes, liquid handlers, and off-the-shelf robotic arms.”)
 If you are wondering what will be left for humans to do when Claude can do everything, you are not alone. Or maybe you are wondering how, aside from becoming a stockholder with voting rights, you’ll have any say in the future that Claude is building for you, humanity, and the planet. Be assured, Anthropic insists, that Claude—here repurposing marketing rhetoric used to describe nearly every other product to come out of Silicon Valley since the nineteen-eighties—is, somehow, good for democracy. In this case, “AI can be used to promote and strengthen democracies and bend the arc of geopolitical history in the direction of freedom.” Nothing in the prospectus, for all its mentions of stopping cyberattacks, provides any real explanation of how this can possibly be true.
 Granted, compared with OpenAI, Google, and Meta , Anthropic is, by far, the most ethically responsible of the leading A.I. companies. Yet its assurances that the Powerful A.I. it plans to develop will be good for democracy—or even, simply, good—involve gobbledygook like this statement (presumably, like Claude’s “constitution,” written at least in part by Claude): “Safety, alignment, and ethical behavior resonate particularly strongly with enterprises, where rigorous safeguards, predictable model behavior, and demonstrable accountability have become decisive criteria in selecting a partner for mission-critical workloads.” And if, instead, the robots go rogue and most humans die —except for a lucky few who, perhaps, find shelter, for centuries, in an atomic-era bunker—the survivors will be able to take comfort in the immortal words of Dr. Strangelove: “There would be no shocking memories, and the prevailing emotion will be one of nostalgia for those left behind, combined with a spirit of bold curiosity for the adventure ahead!”
 Back in 1833, for a small investment in shares costing “not greater than the price of a lottery ticket,” Etzler promised not only extraordinary financial returns but heaven on earth. Within the span of ten years from full investment in his venture, he claimed, “the whole world might therefore be really changed into a paradise.” By the eighteen-forties, he and his followers had scrounged up enough funds to attempt to build this utopia in Venezuela. Using a not yet invented system of intricate machines that could do all things—mechanical automata, or what would now be called robots—there would be “no occasion for any work,” he said, aside from supervising the machines, of course. Alas, in Venezuela, dozens of Etzlerians either died of disease or starvation, or had to be hospitalized owing to deprivation. And, not long after the project’s failure, Etzler simply disappeared.
 Besides its doomed followers, hardly anyone paid much attention to Etzler’s treatise. But, in 1843, after a second edition was printed in London, Henry David Thoreau reviewed it in an American magazine. He mocked Etzler’s schemes and, especially, his arrogance: “We will wash water, and warm fire, and cool ice, and underprop the earth. We will teach birds to fly, and fishes to swim, and ruminants to chew the cud. It is time we had looked into these things.” But, above all, Thoreau questioned Etzler’s equation of human happiness with the increasing speed and efficiency of machines. “Suppose we could compare the moral with the physical, and say how many horse-power the force of love, for instance, blowing on every square foot of a man’s soul, would equal,” Thoreau wrote, two years before he moved to Walden Pond, to live deliberately. He grew gauzy. “Love is the wind, the tide, the waves, the sunshine,” he went on, sticking it, Biblically, to Etzler’s mechanical utopia. “Its power is incalculable; it is many horse-power. It never ceases, it never slacks; it can move the globe without a resting-place; it can warm without fire; it can feed without meat; it can clothe without garments; it can shelter without roof; it can make a paradise within which will dispense with a paradise without.”
 What will more intelligent and more powerful machines mean for humans? “To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” Anthropic concedes. The company promises many good things: better ways to fight disease, shorter lines at the D.M.V. It warns of many bad things: authoritarianism, bioweapons, cyberattacks, the extinction of the human race. How does it measure the benefit to the public? That is to be determined, on the whole, by Anthropic’s seven co-founders, who “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission,” and who, collectively, get 50.1 per cent of general voting power; each has pledged eighty per cent of their personal equity to philanthropy. (An independent long-term-benefit trust separately elects a majority of directors.) What paradise might look like, in other words, is a determination to be made by a very tiny handful of men.
 Artificial intelligence will not usher in a more loving future. Neither will it teach the birds to fly, or the fish to swim. Very little about A.I. has so far augured a better world. And Anthropic, in selling shares in heaven on earth, while issuing warnings about a possible descent into hell, promises nothing so much as a more profane one. ♦
